idiom_name: empty base optimization via private inheritance
implementation_notes: C++ is the pattern's home: the standard exempts base class subobjects from the size-at-least-one rule, so an empty base can be flattened out of the derived object's layout (sizeof(Derived) == sizeof(int) in the canonical example), and the optimization is required for standard-layout types. The portable, standard-guaranteed form is to inherit the stateless policy privately and as the first base, keep it truly empty - no data members, no virtual functions, no virtual bases - and assert the resulting size; private inheritance keeps the policy's members out of the host's public interface, and this is the variant the term 'empty base optimization' refers to. The limits are part of the language: the optimization does not apply when the empty base is also the type (or a base) of the first non-static data member, when the same empty base is inherited more than once, or for virtual bases, and MSVC's default layout needs __declspec(empty_bases) for multiple-inheritance cases. The modern forms are a [[no_unique_address]] member (C++20) and the compressed-pair helper (boost::compressed_pair, std::tuple/std::pair internals).
pitfalls: Adding a data member to the base cancels EBO and changes the ABI; inheriting the same empty base twice, or from it virtually, cancels it too.
Public or protected inheritance leaks the base's names into the host (name lookup runs before access checks) and can change overload resolution or ADL.

Deleting through an empty base pointer with a non-virtual destructor is undefined behaviour even though the base occupies no storage; a protected non-virtual destructor makes that a compile error, while a virtual destructor would cancel the optimization.

variants.name: C++20 [[no_unique_address]] member
variants.implementation_notes: The attribute makes a non-static data member a potentially-overlapping subobject, so an empty member is optimized out exactly like an empty base while the host stays a member-based class: no inheritance, no inherited names, no change to the class hierarchy. Prefer it in C++20 code whenever the stateless policy is conceptually a member; the optimization behaviour matches the base-class rules, including tail-padding reuse.
pitfalls: MSVC ignores [[no_unique_address]] even in C++20 mode; use [[msvc::no_unique_address]] or the type quietly grows.
Two members of the same empty type still need distinct addresses, so each extra same-typed member adds a byte; only the first one is really free.
On compilers without the attribute the program stays correct but the padding returns, so keep the static_assert in the test suite.

variants.name: Compressed-pair helper (library idiom)
variants.implementation_notes: Library form: a small helper template inherits the empty policy and stores one member, exposing accessors, so the host keeps a plain member-based interface while the helper's inheritance chain performs the optimization. It is the technique behind allocator-aware standard containers (std::vector, std::function, std::shared_ptr) and behind the recursive inheritance chains of std::tuple/std::pair implementations; choose it when the policy must stay hidden or when several empty policies are combined.
pitfalls: The helper hides the policy but also complicates construction, assignment and argument forwarding; the initialisation order of base and member must be stated deliberately.
A policy type that is also used as the member type re-introduces the same-type rule and silently loses the saving.
Compressed-pair implementations differ between standard libraries and Boost versions, so the layout is not a stable interface across toolchains.
